topic.subject: science
topic.title: Oxidation, reduction and everyday redox
topic.scope: Oxidation as gain of oxygen or loss of electrons, reduction as the reverse, both occur together, oxidising and reducing agents, rancidity of fats, browning of cut apples, bleaching, displacement reactions

nodes.name: Hydrogen loss is oxidation, gain is reduction
Metal atom loses electrons to form positive ion
Oxidation and reduction occur in the same reaction
Reducing agent is the substance oxidised
Oxidising agent is the substance reduced
Cut fruit browns by oxidation in air
Bleaching removes colour by a chemical change
Reactive metal displaces less reactive metal
In displacement, the reactive metal is oxidised
external_prereqs: colour change as sign of reaction

misconceptions.statement: Oxidation only happens when something burns with a flame.
misconceptions.why: The word is first met with combustion and fire.
misconceptions.fix: Oxidation is any gain of oxygen, and it can be slow, like rusting or an apple turning brown, with no flame.

probe.question: Is the slow rusting of an iron nail oxidation?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because nothing is burning.

misconceptions.root_belief: one familiar example defines the whole idea

misconceptions.statement: Reduction means a substance becomes smaller in amount.
misconceptions.why: In daily language 'reduce' means make less.
misconceptions.fix: Reduction in chemistry means loss of oxygen or gain of hydrogen (or gain of electrons), not a decrease in amount.

probe.question: In CuO + H2 -> Cu + H2O, which substance is reduced?
probe.wrong_answer: Hydrogen, because its amount reduces as it is used up.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of students' use of everyday meanings of chemical terms

misconceptions.statement: Reduction means losing electrons because reduce means lose.
misconceptions.why: The idea of 'less' carries over from the everyday word to electrons.
misconceptions.fix: Reduction is gain of electrons; the atom or ion receiving electrons is reduced.

probe.question: Cu2+ becomes Cu. Is this oxidation or reduction?
probe.wrong_answer: Oxidation, because it has lost its charge.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student difficulties with electron transfer definitions of redox

misconceptions.statement: Oxidation is gain of electrons because oxidation is gain of oxygen.
misconceptions.why: Students carry the word 'gain' from the oxygen definition to electrons.
misconceptions.fix: Oxidation is gain of oxygen but loss of electrons; the two views look opposite but describe the same change.

probe.question: Na becomes Na+. Is sodium oxidised?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it is reduced because it gained a positive charge.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from one context works everywhere
misconceptions.source_hint: concept inventory studies on redox definitions

misconceptions.statement: Adding hydrogen to a substance is oxidation because hydrogen burns.
misconceptions.why: Hydrogen is linked with fire and burning, which is linked with oxidation.
misconceptions.fix: Gain of hydrogen is reduction; loss of hydrogen is oxidation.

probe.question: In H2S + Cl2 -> 2HCl + S, what happens to Cl2?
probe.wrong_answer: It is oxidised because it gains hydrogen.

misconceptions.root_belief: things linked in daily life share one meaning

misconceptions.statement: An atom that loses electrons becomes negatively charged.
misconceptions.why: Students link 'losing' with 'less' and 'negative', ignoring that electrons carry the negative charge.
misconceptions.fix: Electrons are negative, so an atom that loses them is left with extra positive charge and becomes a positive ion.

probe.question: What charge does a magnesium atom get when it loses 2 electrons?
probe.wrong_answer: 2-, because it lost something.

misconceptions.root_belief: losing something makes the result smaller or negative
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student understanding of ions and charge

misconceptions.statement: Oxidation can happen alone, without any reduction.
misconceptions.why: Everyday examples such as rusting show only one substance changing visibly.
misconceptions.fix: Electrons or oxygen lost by one substance must be gained by another, so oxidation and reduction always occur together.

probe.question: Zn is oxidised in a reaction. Must something else be reduced?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only zinc changes.

misconceptions.root_belief: an event happens on its own
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of student ideas on redox as a coupled process

misconceptions.statement: Electrons lost by a substance simply disappear into the air.
misconceptions.why: Electrons cannot be seen, so students think they vanish.
misconceptions.fix: Electrons are never lost to nowhere; they pass from the substance that is oxidised to the substance that is reduced.

probe.question: Where do the electrons lost by iron go when it reacts with copper sulphate?
probe.wrong_answer: They escape into the air.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

misconceptions.statement: The reducing agent is the substance that gets reduced.
misconceptions.why: The names sound like the same thing: reducing agent, reduced.
misconceptions.fix: A reducing agent causes reduction of another substance, and in doing so it is itself oxidised.

probe.question: In CuO + H2 -> Cu + H2O, what is the reducing agent?
probe.wrong_answer: CuO, because it is reduced.

misconceptions.root_belief: similar sounding terms mean the same thing
misconceptions.source_hint: misconception surveys of redox terminology in school chemistry

misconceptions.statement: The oxidising agent is the substance that gets oxidised.
misconceptions.why: The name sounds like the substance itself is oxidised.
misconceptions.fix: An oxidising agent oxidises another substance and is itself reduced.

probe.question: In Mg + CuO -> MgO + Cu, which is the oxidising agent?
probe.wrong_answer: Mg, because it is oxidised.

misconceptions.root_belief: similar sounding terms mean the same thing
misconceptions.source_hint: misconception surveys of redox terminology in school chemistry

misconceptions.statement: Only substances containing oxygen can be oxidising agents.
misconceptions.why: The name 'oxidising' suggests oxygen must be present.
misconceptions.fix: Any substance that takes electrons from another can oxidise it, for example chlorine, which has no oxygen.

probe.question: Can chlorine gas act as an oxidising agent?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because it has no oxygen.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from an early definition works everywhere

misconceptions.statement: Fats and oils turn rancid because germs grow in them.
misconceptions.why: Students think all food going bad is caused by microbes.
misconceptions.fix: Rancidity is mainly the slow oxidation of fats and oils by oxygen in air, giving a bad smell and taste.

probe.question: What causes the bad smell in old cooking oil?
probe.wrong_answer: Bacteria growing in the oil.

misconceptions.root_belief: spoilage is always caused by living germs
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of children's ideas about decay and microbes

misconceptions.statement: Only butter and ghee can become rancid, not packed snacks.
misconceptions.why: The usual examples in daily life are dairy fats.
misconceptions.fix: Any food with fats or oils, such as chips, namkeen and cooking oil, can become rancid.

probe.question: Can a packet of fried namkeen become rancid?
probe.wrong_answer: No, rancidity affects only butter and ghee.

misconceptions.root_belief: a few familiar examples cover the whole idea

misconceptions.statement: Nitrogen is put in chip packets to kill germs.
misconceptions.why: Students assume all preservation means killing germs.
misconceptions.fix: Nitrogen is unreactive and pushes out oxygen, so the fats in the chips are not oxidised and do not turn rancid.

probe.question: Why is nitrogen gas filled in a chips packet?
probe.wrong_answer: To kill bacteria.

misconceptions.root_belief: spoilage is always caused by living germs

misconceptions.statement: A cut apple turns brown because it dries out in the air.
misconceptions.why: The visible change happens on the exposed surface, so students assume drying.
misconceptions.fix: Chemicals in the cut apple react with oxygen from air, which is oxidation, forming brown substances.

probe.question: Why does a cut apple turn brown?
probe.wrong_answer: Its surface dries out.

misconceptions.root_belief: only visible changes matter, not chemical ones
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of children's explanations of everyday chemical changes

misconceptions.statement: Iron rusts only when it is in water.
misconceptions.why: Rust is usually seen on things wet with rain.
misconceptions.fix: Rusting needs both oxygen (air) and water; with only one of them, iron does not rust.

probe.question: Will an iron nail rust in boiled water covered with a layer of oil?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it is in water.

misconceptions.root_belief: one event has one single cause
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of student explanations of rusting conditions

misconceptions.statement: A rusted iron nail weighs less than the original nail.
misconceptions.why: Students think rotting or burning wears material away.
misconceptions.fix: Iron combines with oxygen to form rust, so the rusted iron is heavier than the iron it started with.

probe.question: A clean iron nail is allowed to rust completely. What happens to its mass?
probe.wrong_answer: It decreases because the iron is eaten away.

misconceptions.root_belief: things that burn or decay lose matter
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student ideas about mass change in burning and rusting

misconceptions.statement: Bleach removes colour only by physically washing the dye away.
misconceptions.why: Students link cleaning with washing and do not see a chemical change.
misconceptions.fix: Bleaching agents react chemically with the coloured substance, usually by oxidising it so it turns colourless.

probe.question: How does bleaching powder remove a stain?
probe.wrong_answer: It dissolves and washes the colour off without any reaction.

misconceptions.root_belief: a visible change is only a physical change

misconceptions.statement: A heavier or denser metal displaces a lighter metal from its salt solution.
misconceptions.why: Students use physical properties such as heaviness as a sign of strength.
misconceptions.fix: Displacement depends on reactivity, not on mass or density; a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one.

probe.question: Lead is heavier than zinc. Will lead displace zinc from zinc sulphate?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because lead is heavier.

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or heavier means more effect

misconceptions.statement: Any metal placed in any salt solution will displace the metal in it.
misconceptions.why: Students generalise from the one example they have seen, iron in copper sulphate.
misconceptions.fix: A metal displaces another only if it is more reactive; copper cannot displace zinc or iron from their salts.

probe.question: Will a copper strip displace zinc from zinc sulphate solution?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the copper will replace the zinc.

misconceptions.root_belief: reactions always happen when substances meet
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of student overgeneralisation of single displacement reactions

misconceptions.statement: When an iron nail turns copper coloured in copper sulphate, the iron has turned into copper.
misconceptions.why: Students see the nail change colour and assume the substance itself changed.
misconceptions.fix: Iron atoms go into the solution as ions and copper ions take electrons from the nail and deposit as a layer of copper; iron never becomes copper.

probe.question: What is the brown coating on an iron nail dipped in copper sulphate?
probe.wrong_answer: The iron itself has changed into copper.

misconceptions.root_belief: one substance can turn into another
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student ideas about chemical change and transmutation

misconceptions.statement: Oxidation cannot occur if oxygen is not present.
misconceptions.why: Students hold on to the first definition they learnt and ignore the electron view.
misconceptions.fix: Oxidation is also loss of electrons, so it can happen without oxygen, as when sodium reacts with chlorine.

probe.question: Is Na + Cl2 -> NaCl an oxidation reaction for sodium?
probe.wrong_answer: No, there is no oxygen in it.

misconceptions.root_belief: the first definition learnt is the complete one
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of student difficulties moving between oxygen and electron definitions of redox
